# Reverse-a-function drill — 2026-10-10
Target: Windows x86-64 (arg in `ecx`, return in `al`/`eax`).
Reverse this short function to equivalent C:
```asm mystery: sub ecx, 48 xor eax, eax cmp ecx, 9 setbe al ret ```
What does `mystery(int c)` compute? Why is there only one comparison, and why `setbe` rather than `setle`?
---
## Answer
```c int mystery(int c) { return (unsigned)(c - '0') <= 9; // isdigit-style range check } ```
## Explanation
- 48 is `'0'`; subtracting it maps `'0'..'9'` to `0..9`, and anything below `'0'` wraps to a huge unsigned value. - `setbe` (CF=1 or ZF=1) is an *unsigned* compare, so one `cmp` rejects both too-small and too-large inputs, replacing `c >= '0' && c <= '9'`. - `xor eax,eax` comes before `cmp` because xor would clobber the flags; `setbe` writes only `al`, so the upper bits stay 0.
